speaker: Warren E. Burger
text: 70-112, Groppi against Leslie.

speaker: Warren E. Burger

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: Mr. Chief Justice and may it please the Court.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: This matter is before the Court on a petition for a Writ of Certiorari United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: The pertinent facts out of which this matter arose are as follows.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: On October 1, 1969 the Assembly, one of the two Houses of the State of Wisconsin legislature passed a resolution reciting that two days earlier on September 29th, 1969, the petitioner led a gathering of the people which by its presence on the floor of the Assembly during a meeting prevented the Assembly from conducting its business.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: The resolution found the petitioner's conduct constituted disorderly conduct in the immediate view of the House and directly tending to interrupt its proceedings.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: The resolution then cited the petitioner for contempt and ordered that he be imprisoned in the Dane County Jail for a period of six months or for the balance of the legislative session whichever was briefer.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: Petitioner was given no notice of the charge against him and was given no hearing of any kind, either before the resolution was passed or after the resolution was passed.

speaker: Warren E. Burger
text: Was the petitioner taken in to custody in the house itself where the disorder was --?

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: No your honor.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: Chief Justice, the disturbance had occurred two days previously and --

speaker: Warren E. Burger
text: What I was asking, was there any effort to take him into custody at the time he was on the floor?

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: None at all.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: At the time, the resolution was passed, the petitioner was in fact incarcerated in the Dane County Jail under a disorderly conduct charge which had been placed against him arising out of the same conduct dealt with the legislative resolution.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: The petitioner was served with copy of the resolution and he was then confined in the Dane County Jail pursuant to the authority of the resolution.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: After this, he was served with the copy of the resolution, he instituted various legal actions contesting the constitutionality of the procedures employed by the legislature in imprisoning him for six months.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: Writs of Habeas Corpus were denied by the Circuit Court of Dane County and by the Wisconsin Supreme Court.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: A petition for writ of habeas corpus was filed in the United State District Court for the Western District of Wisconsin.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: A response was filed and the District Court thereupon released the petitioner on bail, pending the determination of the writ of habeas corpus.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: Bail had been denied to the petitioner by both the Circuit Court of Dane County and by the Wisconsin Supreme Court.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: All of the petitions for habeas corpus filed by the petitioner alleged that he had been denied Due Process law and that he had been denied the right to be represented by counsel, the right to a trial or a hearing of any kind, the right to compulsory process.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: The right to be informed of the nature and cause of the accusation against him.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: The right to confront his accusers and the right to present his defense, the alleged charges.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: On April 8th, 1970 the District Court held that the legislative assembly could not summarily impose a jail sentence for a legislative contempt without first providing the petitioner some minimal opportunity to appear and respond to the charge.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: The Court granted the writ and ordered the petitioner, release under any further restrain or custody pursuant to the resolution.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: The respondent appealed the decision of the District Court of Seventh Circuit Court of Appeals and on appeal the judgment of the District Court was reversed.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: Subsequently the Court of Appeals granted petitioner's request for re-hearing on bond and in a 4:3 decision affirmed the earlier decision of the Court of Appeals.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: The issues presented on the appeal are whether a legislative body can consistent with due process law two days after alleged contemptuous conduct, ex parte impersonate person under its contempt power without giving the person any notice of the charge against him or any opportunity, whatsoever to appear before the legislative body and respond to the charges.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: The second issue is whether consistent with a due process clause, a person can be found in contempt to the legislative body when the contempt resolutions sets forth mere conclusion and failed to set forth any of the underlying facts and circumstances which constituted the alleged contemptuous behavior.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: The petitioner respectfully contend that the Wisconsin legislature did not have the power to summarily punish for contempt.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: The petitioner --

speaker: unknown
text: Back to your second point.

speaker: unknown

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: Yes, that may well is a violation of the rule where we would probably proceed on some basis that as we have been indicated here, we have proceeded throughout these proceedings that the legislature of the state of Wisconsin like all legislatures has a contempt power.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: The question is what is the scope for that contempt power and what procedures must they follow in exercising the contempt power.

speaker: Warren E. Burger
text: I suppose the disorderly conduct charges never then pursued.

speaker: Warren E. Burger

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: No, Chief Justice and as a matter of fact, the day prior to the passing of this resolution by the assembly.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: The petitioner had, in fact, then charged with disorderly conduct, he in fact, after the resolution was issued had a jury trial on that charge of disorderly conduct and after the jury had deliberated and was unable to return a verdict.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: The trial Court granted the defendants motions for dismissal or judgment of acquittal which he had taken under advisement at the conclusion of all the cases.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: He, in fact, successfully defended the criminal disorderly conduct charge.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: In regard to the summary contempt powers, Courts have clearly exercised summary contempt policy.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: However, the decisions of this Court have always limited the exercise to the exercise of that power to those situations where the misconduct is actually observed by the Court and where immediate punishment was necessary to restore order and maintain the dignity and authority of the Court because of the dangers inherent in the summary contempt power which has been described as perhaps nearest akin to despotic power of any power existing under our form of Government, this Court has construed it as an exception to the normal requirements of Due process and has refused to extend it particularly in Johnson versus Mississippi, Mayberry versus Pennsylvania.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: The summary power has never before in the history of this country prior to October 1, 1969 ever been exercised by a legislative body.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: A good reason exists for not extending that power to the legislature.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: First, and I think foremost, Courts differ significantly from legislatures.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: It is the duty and the business of Courts to determine and decide particular cases free from the exercise of the external influences as Judge Stevens noted in his dissenting opinion on the unbound hearing without reflecting adversely on the importance and dignity of the legislative function.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: It must be recognized that legislators are more responsive to the temporary moods of the body politics than our judges.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: And further in this case, in Johnson v. Mississippi, this Court held that a judge who was so enmeshed in matters involved was so enmeshed that matters involving a defendant that it was appropriate for another judge to seat and determine the question of this contempt and indicate noting that the trial before an unbiased judge was essential to due process.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: In this case given the responsiveness of the body power or legislatures through the pressures or the mood, in particular political mood at the time, I do not think you could view the Wisconsin assembly at this point as an unbiased judge.

speaker: William M. Coffey

speaker: Potter Stewart

speaker: William M. Coffey

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: Secondly in terms of the legislative contempt, the physical contours of most legislative chambers along with the comings and goings of the people in the legislature during the session, the absence of transcribed records make it reasonable as the District Court found and as Judge Stevens noted in his dissenting opinion that there is the room for error in perception and evaluation of the alleged contemptuous conduct is far greater and in a legislative body then before a court in the restricted area in which a court may make a summary contempt finding.

text: Whether it may in a words of the Terry case cited in our brief proceed upon its own knowledge of the facts and punish the offender without further proof and without issue or trial in any form.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: This is as we pointed out to a Court Appeals was a “not a non-issue of fact,” that the District Court assumed to determine without giving the State an opportunity to prove in an evidentiary hearing, that in fact the legislators who did vote for the contempt resolution were in fact present on the day that the contempt took place and were in fact those who voted for the contempt resolution?

speaker: Potter Stewart
text: Well, I thought the whole point of the petitioner's second preposition was that until there was a detailed statement of what the alleged content consisted of that people voting on the contempt would have known what it was and the implication of that is that there were not there.

speaker: Potter Stewart
text: They did not see it with their own eyes two days earlier.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: I do not understand that to be petitioner's argument that maybe what he is driving at--

speaker: Potter Stewart
text: That is by implication what his argument has to depend upon?

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: I interpreted petitioner’s argument to be that the resolution failed to State sufficient probable cause as this Court has interpreted probable cause and this appears in Judge Kiley (ph) dissent in the Court of Appeals.

speaker: Potter Stewart
text: It sets forth mere conclusion and fails to set forth any underlying facts and circumstances which constitute the alleged contemptuous behavior and I assume that the implication of that whole argument is that there where people who voted on this who did not see this with their own eyes.

speaker: Potter Stewart
text: Otherwise the argument does not --.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: I have never—

speaker: Potter Stewart
text: I thought that point did raise the factual issue.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: I have never understood that to be petitioner’s argument.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: There was no such an allegation in the original petition in the District Court.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: This sort of recitation of fact as to who voted and who saw has never appeared to my knowledge in any resolution of contempt passed by any legislative body at anytime and it has never been required by any Court at anytime.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: This I see as a non issue I take it to be conceded.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: I believe it to be conceded by the petitioner that a legislative body such as State House of the State Legislature has the power to punish.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: It is house having authority to commit for contempt.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: For example, precedent for that is the cases cited in both briefs, I take it to be a non issue that there have been very grave and serious abuses of the parliamentary powers of contempt in past.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: The amicus brief dwells at some length on this and I am certain that if there had been search made even more grievous abuses could have been cited than were cited in the briefs.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: However I do not see that as an issue in this case because what is happened in the past, this Court has said that simple abuses of the power are no reason for denying its existence.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: Another thing that is conceded and is not at issue in this case, is that the contempt power and particularly the summary contempt power is an extremely delicate power to be used sparingly as this Court has said and is to be exercised with the greatest sense of responsibility, this is conceded.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: There is an other non issue in this case and that is the constitutionality of Wisconsin’s legislative Contempt Statute.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: That is the statute that was referred to by counsel, Section 1326.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: The issue of the constitutionality of that statute was litigated in a companion case to this one.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: The Freylik case and their a three Judge District Court ruled that the statute constitutional that it was not big over broad, that it did not call for involuntary servitude and other issues.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: There was no appeal from that decision by the Three Judge District Court.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: This case incidentally is a spin off from that case. This case started as the federal civil rights action for Declaratory Judgment and then when the Federal District Judge ruled that the portion of that action, the request for an injunction actually was a request for habeas corpus relief then this case Groppi versus Leslie became a spin off of Groppi versus Frelly and proceeded as a habeas case.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: It is also conceded and I see it to be a non issue in this case that a legislative body has other courses, it may fallow in the event of a direct disorderly contempt of its proceedings.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: It may refer the matter to the Courts.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: In the Watkins case, this Court observed that Congress has rarely exercised its contempt powers but had preferred at that time to refer matters of contempt to the United State Attorney for prosecution.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: There is no issue about this.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: The legislative --

speaker: William J. Brennan, Jr.
text: (Inaudible) to expressly authorize --

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: Yes, it had.

speaker: William J. Brennan, Jr.
text: That is not the 13.72?

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: Yes, 13 that is what I am referring to.

speaker: William J. Brennan, Jr.
text: Well, this applied only in the case of one, actually a judge guilty by the house?

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: Yes, I am sorry Mr. Justice Brennan.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: What I was think of was the disorderly conduct statute.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: Yes, disorderly conduct occurring anywhere within the State maybe prosecuted and the legislative -- the assembly could have treated this simply as a case of disorderly conduct.

speaker: William J. Brennan, Jr.
text: Under the general statute?

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: Yes, under general statute.

speaker: William J. Brennan, Jr.
text: But federal statute is expressed is it not?

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: Yes.

speaker: William J. Brennan, Jr.
text: It authorizes reference expressly in the case that contempts found by the house.

speaker: William J. Brennan, Jr.
text: That is required to make a federal statue first is it not?

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: It is, and what I should say is Wisconsin has no parallel to that statute.

speaker: Thurgood Marshall
text: Was it -- the disorderly conduct at this time on same about same business?

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: No.

speaker: Thurgood Marshall
text: Or is that a different affair?

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: That the arrest was made, as I remember was made at the later time.

speaker: Warren E. Burger
text: For conduct occurring where?

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: On the assembly floor.

speaker: Warren E. Burger
text: That it was the same conduct?

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: Yes, the same conduct.

speaker: Warren E. Burger
text: Your response I think was a little confusing.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: I am sorry.

speaker: Warren E. Burger
text: Just to make sure we have it clear.

speaker: Warren E. Burger
text: It was at time of contempt citation, he was in custody on a disorderly conduct charge for the same conduct that the legislature was deeming with.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: Exactly the same.

speaker: Warren E. Burger
text: And that is the case that ended in a mistrial and it was followed by dismissal?

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: That is correct.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: I am sorry, I did not intent to mislead.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: It is exactly the same conduct that was tried in the disorderly conduct case under the general statute.

speaker: Potter Stewart
text: It was just under a charge he had been not convict?

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: That is correct.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: He was never convicted of disorderly conduct in the Court.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: There as Mr. Chief Justice Burger point it out there never was a -- there was a mistrial and never any new trial.

speaker: Potter Stewart
text: There the charge still hanging over him now, would it?

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: Conceivably there could be a charge under section 13.27 of the statutes.

speaker: Potter Stewart
text: There was a mistrial but it was charge ever dismissed?

speaker: Potter Stewart
text: Yes, it was dismissed.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: It was dismissed.

speaker: unknown
text: Well 13.27 requires a prior resolution to the convicting and contempt with the legislature?

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: Yes, Sir.

speaker: unknown
text: For this case it was –

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: The State has never contented that it is moot.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: I would feel that as long as the possibility exists, that someone could prefer charges under section 1327.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: I would feel that under Grafus versus Low Valley that the there was sufficient interest left here in the petitioner and a sufficient hazard involved at least theoretically.

speaker: unknown
text: Is the facts limitations applicable to that 1327 type?

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: I know of none.

speaker: unknown
text: But certainly there would be extremely almost insurmountable double jeopardy problems too?

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: Absolutely.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: That is my opinion.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: It is not an issue here but that would be my opinion.

speaker: unknown
text: Well if that so, why do you not urge this?

speaker: William J. Brennan, Jr.
text: If we sustain that a resolution that you want us to do -- and that there was a problem of double jeopardy, nothing else could happen anyway.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: That is correct.

speaker: William J. Brennan, Jr.
text: So, sort of an empty argument is it not?

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: As I understand Carafas versus LaVallee and the principles in that case, if there is a theoretical possibility that a previous judgment if allowed to stand could work to someone’s disadvantage in the future, then the issue is not moot.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: So we certainly have not urged.

speaker: unknown
text: It was because its advantage is it could not be tried.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: But that issue is not before the Court at this time and all I can say is that in my personal opinion, yes.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: There would be –-

speaker: unknown
text: New argument on that ground.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: I do not believe under the cases that have been decided by this Court that I cannot argue on -- I am not urging that.

speaker: unknown
text: In other word you are not arguing would --?

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: I am not.

speaker: unknown
text: This is why I raised the question with Mr. Coffey a little while ago.

speaker: unknown
text: I want to be sure about your position.

speaker: unknown
text: You are not arguing this?

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: That is correct.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: It is also a non issue in this case that the assembly could have taken different courses of action as Congress has the power to take different courses of action in contempt cases.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: The question before this Court is whether the constitution requires that the legislative body must take some different course of action.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: Whether it must refrain and ignore the contempt altogether or whether it must rely on general criminal statutes or whether it must somehow refer the matter to the executive and rely upon the executive or upon the judiciary to vindicate its authority.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: It is also a non issue in this case that if this had been a case of indirect or constructive contempt, obviously the procedure followed by the assembly would have been invalid.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: Good many of the case cited in both of the briefs, in petitioner's brief or respondent's brief refer to cases of indirect constructive contempt where the legislative bodies have brought the contemnor before the bar of the house or of the Senate and there have heard evidence of what occurred outside the Legislative (Inaudible).

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: These are constructive contempt cases.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: This is not, this is direct contempt case involving the disorderly conduct.

speaker: Thurgood Marshall
text: Is anything in the record to show why the resolution was not passed the same day?

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: None.

speaker: unknown
text: Well, there is an indication in the opinion of the Supreme Court of the State based on judicial notice that the legislature could not act that day.

speaker: unknown
text: There was so much disruption.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: Yes.

speaker: Warren E. Burger
text: 12 Noon until approximately midnight, the legislature was in effect ousted of its own chamber. Is that not the case on this record?

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: That appears in the record.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: There has been no evidentiary hearing so that it has not been developed in that fashion.

speaker: Thurgood Marshall
text: What happened the next day?

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: I would have to go outside the record to tell you Mr. Justice Marshall.

speaker: Thurgood Marshall
text: I do not want to go outside the record, I just want to know as anything in the record to show why it took two days?

speaker: Thurgood Marshall
text: We now have one day explained but there is no explanation for the next day?

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: Nothing.

speaker: Thurgood Marshall
text: Is there anything in the record to show what was brought before the house or is it just the resolution?

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: There is --

speaker: Thurgood Marshall
text: or is it discussion?

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: There is nothing in the record to show the debate that is not recited in the resolution.

speaker: unknown
text: Was it two days, September 29th and October 1st over a weekend?

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: September 29th was a Monday, that was the day on which the legislature was to convene in special session.

speaker: unknown
text: So it was right at the start of session?

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: It was right at the start of the session.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: As a matter fact, I cannot say that it was at the start of the session because the session did not start on the day that it was to have started.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: I have talked about the none issues and the issue as I see it again is a very narrow one.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: Does the constitution command that a legislative body exercise its contempt power different from the manner in which a Court is entitled to exercise the same power.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: There are no cases in point, at least neither of the parties to this action have been able to find a case precisely in point.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: Most cases discussing legislative contempt incidents of the legislative contempt are cases of constructive or indirect contempt.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: Whereas as I said previously the contemnor is brought before the bar because the house has not seen the conduct with its own eyes.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: In some of the precedents, some of the cases discussing legislative contempts, it is apparent that a summary procedure was in fact followed but there has never been any discussion of that in any of the cases that have a reason.

speaker: unknown
text: Would Wisconsin's position be the same if a lapse of time instead of two day, it is two months?

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: I think yes.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: Wisconsin’s case would be much weaker.

speaker: unknown
text: Why would it be weaker on the issue at the appendix?

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: Because without anything in the record to explain the delay.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: I think there would be, It would just be that much more difficult to explain a delay of that magnitude.

speaker: unknown
text: I did not understand what Wisconsin's position was instead of --

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: We do not -- not as far as the two days are concerned.

speaker: unknown
text: I do not understand why if you do not have to explain this two days, you would have explain it two months.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: I believe in the first place that there have been instances, decisions by this Court, for example in the Terry case, ex parte Terry, In Re Morrey (ph) which is a second circuit case, that there have been delays unexplained in the record.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: And this Court has said that short delays do not have to be explained.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: For example, in the Terry case I believe there was delay of one day.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: The disorderly conduct occurred in open Court on one day and the contempt citation did not come out for the next day.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: Court said this delay is frivolous.

speaker: Warren E. Burger
text: There has been some reference to the procedure followed by Judge Medina in the contempt cases that occurred during prolonged trial in New York, years ago.

speaker: Warren E. Burger
text: Now, suppose hypothetically that the legislature decided deliberately to postpone the action on the contempt until the last day of the session or last week of the session in order to let tempers cool and get a more objective view, would that be a perfectly valid reason for waiting 30 days or 60 days or 90 days and who is to complain about that kind of a delay for that reason?

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: Well, if you delay to that extent.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: That would seem to undermine the assembly’s position that it needed protection.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: That it had the authority to remove this source of disturbance.

speaker: Warren E. Burger
text: That is only one of the reasons for the contempt powers.

speaker: Warren E. Burger
text: is it not?

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: Yes.

speaker: Warren E. Burger
text: It is not the whole basis for giving legislative body contempt power?

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: It is not.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: There is self reservation and there is what has been called by the Courts of indication of the body’s authority--

speaker: Warren E. Burger
text: Taking example of someone as a deterrent to similar future conduct by others?

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: I think the juror has never been mentioned in any case that I have seen but I think as matter of logic and common sense, yes deterrence plays very large part in this.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: There was a case, where the United State Senate proceeded summarily and ex parte Nugent cited in the respondent's brief where the debate and the deliberations leading up to the contempt resolution and the contempt resolution itself were conducted in secret.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: There again, and the Circuit Court for the District of Columbia at that time held that this was a proper procedure but the precise point that we have here, that is whether or not the legislature has any less power than the Courts around the nation to proceed in a proper case in summary fashion has never been expressly discussed and decided by any Court.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: The closest decision that I know that it comes to it is Marshall versus Gordon.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: There, there is some dictum that suggests that the power -- that the Courts have to exercise summary contempt powers proceeds from the same source and that both the legislators and the Courts have identical summary contempt powers.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: The District Judge said “alright there are no cases, there is nothing to guide this Court, I am going to look to see if there are any reasons in logic or in the factual circumstances of the two bodies” that is the Court and legislature to warrant a different treatment before the law.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: And the District Judge said,” well, there are so many people observing disorderly conduct in the legislative chamber, that you can have a good deal of confusion as to just what took place whereas in the Court, you have only one Judge looking and it is easier if you would not have that confusion”.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: The District Judge said also, there is a second point, that there is no transcript of the proceeding in a legislative chamber whereas there is in Court.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: And on those two points, the District Court held that the legislature did not have summary contempt powers.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: The Seventh Circuit Court of Appeals disagreed and I think rightly so because if it is true that one pair of eyes is better than several pairs of eyes, then of course one juror better than many jurors.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: Appellate Courts, for example, would not be able to observe properly, according to the District Judge's theory, would not be able to observe a direct contempt.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: The differences that are pointed out in the respondent's brief between Courts and legislatures are such that the legislature should have summary contempt powers at least equal to those possessed by the Courts, because there are probably upward to 5000 Judges in this country who posses summary contempt powers.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: There are only 50 legislatures.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: When you stop a legislature, there is no other body that can pick up the ball and run with it and do the work of that that legislature.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: It stops.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: And a continual week by week disturbance in the legislature would forever stop that legislature.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: Further more, a legislative body when it is proceeding to act upon a contempt, acts publicly.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: There is publicity, there is deliberation.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: Usually, in the two party political system you can expect debate before action is taken.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: There are certainly similarities between legislatures and courts that again call for similar treatment, similar powers of self reservation.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: They have been cited. Cases have been cited going back to parliamentary times in England, Colonial times in this country.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: Anderson versus Dunn, up to Marshall versus Gordon, Jurney v. MacCracken, where this court has said the legislature is just as vulnerable as any Court to attack in disruption.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: It has also been acknowledged by this Court many times that it is essential to preserve the independence of the legislative body and you cannot force the legislature to rely upon the -- sometimes hostile Judiciary or an unfriendly executive taking those words from United States versus Johnson.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: There is certainly a need on the part of legislature as great as in the Courts to continue functioning and to continue the dialog that takes place in a legislature.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: There are no differences that warrant a denial of this power to legislature and the similarities between the two forums, to call for and demonstrate that both bodies must have equal powers to protect themselves from attack.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: The contempt power is certainly very – it is a radical power, it is drastic, it is subject to great abuse and it is very properly limited and back in 1848, the Wisconsin legislature did very severely limit the contempt power of the Houses of Legislature.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: It described a very-very narrow area in which the legislature could act upon a direct contempt. Only where there has been disorderly conduct on the floor of the House, in the immediate view of the House in which directly tends to disrupt, can the legislature act summarily.

speaker: Sverre O. Tinglum
text: Thank you.

speaker: Warren E. Burger
text: Thank you.

speaker: Warren E. Burger
text: You have four minutes left Mr. Coffey.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: Mr. Chief Justice, the inquiry, the respondent has preceded that the summary contempt power is very great power subject to abuse.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: In the instance case, there is no way that the petitioner has ever been able to get a review, the factual basis on which the legislature asked.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: The Wisconsin Supreme Court in denying the petition to writ habeas corpus suggested that some type of judicial review was available.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: We filed a motion of petition for rehearing in the Wisconsin Supreme Court, and requested -- indicated that their opinion indicated such a judicial review was available.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: All of the authority that we had found indicated to contrary, would the Court please advise the petitioner, what kind of hearing was available to him and grant him that hearing, but even assuming that he could have gotten the hearing at that time, I think we must recognize that hearing comes too late.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: The petitioner was already in jail pursuant to the contempt resolution and at that point he had been denied bail and I do not believe that he should have his right to a hearing on the factual basis of the contempt after he is already in jail.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: I think, the hearing should precede the right of anyone to place him in custody.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: I suggest that as the District Court held that at a very minimum, the petitioner was entitled to be given notice of the charges against him and be given an opportunity to respond to them.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: Thank you.

speaker: Warren E. Burger
text: Mr. Coffey do you suggest that judicial review of a legislative contempt determination would be available, for example on the weight of the evidence or just on procedural regularity?

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: I would suggest Mr. Chief Justice that it has to be available on both or there would be no basis on which to check the arbitrary exercised power by the legislature.

speaker: Warren E. Burger
text: What you are suggesting on is that the judicial branch would have the power to re-determine the fact as distinguished from passing merely on procedural regularity of the contempt process?

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: I think that is essential Mr. Chief Justice.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: Or there is no check on completely arbitrary incarceration of people that these please the legislative body and there has to be a check on that kind of party.

speaker: Warren E. Burger
text: Very well.

speaker: unknown
text: Is that not what the Supreme Court of Wisconsin said is available, on page 23 (a) of the appendix?

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: The Wisconsin –

speaker: unknown
text: The Wisconsin seems to say that is what is available and that the review of procedure is not available, and as the only issues presented that dealt primarily with procedure, not with issue of his innocence or with the merits of any defense implying that had they have you presented problems on the merits, they would review it.

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: They did suggest that which is contrary as the District Court opinion noted was contrary to the existing case, warned Wisconsin at the time and when the petitioner asked for that hearing the motion for rehearing was denied without hearing and without comment.

speaker: Warren E. Burger
text: Is it not contrary to the general line of authority in both the English and the early American cases also, the review of the merits?

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: Yes it is Mr. Chief Justice.

speaker: Warren E. Burger
text: So this was probably reasonably false in the category dicta by the Court in the Wisconsin case, does it not?

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: Either that or an overruling of other authority without expressly doing.

speaker: Warren E. Burger
text: And where it was not necessary to reach the point?

speaker: William M. Coffey
text: No.

speaker: Warren E. Burger
text: Thank you Mr. Coffey.

speaker: Warren E. Burger
text: Thank you gentleman.

speaker: Warren E. Burger
text: The case is submitted.
